Metabolic measurements obtained under controlled laboratory conditions provide insight into the energetic demands of the Alpine field mouse (Apodemus alpicola). At a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the resting metabolic rate reaches 87.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 87.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the substantial thermoregulatory costs associated with inhabiting high-altitude environments. This elevated oxygen consumption is consistent with patterns observed in other small mammals native to alpine zones, where cold ambient temperatures require sustained heat production even during periods of inactivity. The measurements were taken from individuals acclimated to laboratory conditions for several weeks, ensuring that the recorded rates represent basal rather than stress-induced metabolism. Comparative data from lowland congeners suggest that this metabolic intensity may be an adaptation to the short, cool summers and long winters characteristic of the species' natural range in the European Alps.

Reproductive output in the Alpine field mouse is characterized by relatively modest litter sizes and a constrained breeding season. Females typically produce three pups per litter [N_R_i = three pups per litter], a figure that aligns closely with values documented in the closely related wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus). Across the breeding season, which lasts approximately four months under alpine conditions, females may produce up to three litters annually [F_R_i = up to three litters annually]. At a mean nest temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], this reproductive schedule yields a moderate annual reproductive rate that balances the energetic costs of lactation against the brief window of favorable conditions. The relatively modest litter size likely reflects a trade-off between offspring quality and number, given the short growing season available for juvenile development before winter onset.

Neonatal development proceeds rapidly in this species, a necessity imposed by the abbreviated alpine growing season. Newborn pups weigh approximately 2.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.5 grams] at parturition, a mass comparable to that reported for Apodemus sylvaticus from which the estimate is derived. At a nest temperature maintained near 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], these altricial neonates are entirely dependent on maternal care during the early postnatal period. The relatively low birth mass, representing roughly eight percent of the ultimate adult female mass, is typical of small murid rodents and necessitates an extended period of rapid growth and thermoregulatory development. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of 32.56 grams [Wwi = 32.56 grams], a size that is achieved only after several months of growth and that confers advantages in terms of both reproductive output and overwinter survival.

Life-history timing follows a predictable sequence when measured under controlled thermal conditions. Gestation lasts approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days] at a mean maternal body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], a duration that is consistent with values reported for other members of the genus Apodemus and may reflect the constraints of alpine environments where extended gestation periods could reduce the number of litters produced within a short season. Following parturition, the young are weaned at 17 days after birth [tx = 17 days after birth] when maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], marking the transition to nutritional independence, which is a relatively brief nursing period that allows females to potentially initiate a subsequent reproductive event within the same season. The interval from birth to the attainment of sexual maturity is 71 days [tp = 71 days] under the same thermal regime, enabling individuals born early in the season to potentially breed before the onset of winter.

This relatively extended lifespan for a small rodent is noteworthy and may reflect the low extrinsic mortality rates characteristic of high-altitude environments, where predation pressure is reduced and seasonal activity is compressed. Field records suggest that most individuals in natural populations survive for considerably shorter periods, with the majority succumbing during their first winter. The balanced combination of a birth mass representing about eight percent of the adult mass with a potential six-year maximum lifespan underscores the slow pace of life in this alpine specialist compared to lowland murids.
